newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK industry must embrace change to flourish - study.
newsitem.headline: HK industry must embrace change to flourish - study.

text.p: Hong Kong could get a new lease on life as a manufacturing centre if industry and the government were willing to invest more in research and development, a study by a U.S. university found.

"Hong Kong has the potential to emerge as a world leader in producing service-enhanced manufactured products," said Richard Lester, director of the MIT Industrial Performance Center and co-leader of the study.

"But to construct such a future, it cannot rely only on these strengths it has acquired during 40 years of rapid industrial expansion. Hong Kong also must address a critical set of weaknesses in its current system," said Lester.
Over the years, Hong Kong manufacturers have relocated production to where the price of land and labour is lower, with many shifting production to nearby Guangdong province in China.
As a result, the percentage of the territory's gross domestic product attributable to products "Made in Hong Kong" has fallen to just 9.3 percent of GDP from 23-24 percent a decade ago.

However, the contribution to the territory's wealth of products "Made by Hong Kong" -- where the companies are owned and operated by Hong Kong enterprises but goods are produced elsewhere -- has grown considerably, the U.S. researchers found.

Moreover, "much of the service sector in Hong Kong is dedicated to serving those manufacturing activities through transport, financial and telecommunication services, as well as thorough other services such as design and even advertising," said Lester.

With land and labour prices rising in Guangdong and other areas of China, Hong Kong manufacturers will need to shift their focus, learning new technologies that will allow them to add value to products by improving services associated with them.
But the obstacles are daunting, the researchers said.
For example, Hong Kong spends a dismal 0.1 percent of GDP on research and development, compared with 2.9 percent in Japan, 2.4 percent in the U.S. and 1.2 percent in Singapore.
Even China spends more, devoting 0.5 percent of GDP to research in technology.
The education system also is failing to deliver adequately trained personnel, with scant links between what universities offer and what industry needs.
The study made several recommendations for Hong Kong to improve its own research and development capabilities, as well as to help attract technology from abroad.
Assuring intellectual copyright protection and establishing decentralised science parks for start-up, small-technology based enterprises were among the recommendations.
Other Asian countries, notably Singapore, have been aggressive in offering incentives to technology-based industries. But the researchers cautioned that Hong Kong should not follow Singapore's model.

"Hong Kong has a really vibrant sector of small and medium-scale enterprises which we see as the driving force in development," said Suzanne Berger, co-lead of the project and director of the MIT International Science and Technology Initiative/China Program.
She said these enterprises can benefit from embracing new technology on a small scale, or by pooling capabilities with other firms.

Singapore has focused on attracting high technology multi-national corporations, "which has had a positive effect on increasing the skill level of the workforce but has not invigorated the small and medium-sized sectors," added Lester.
Hong Kong would be better served by focusing on broad efforts to improve technological capabilities of the population rather than by targeting specific sectors, the researchers said.
